header:
Date: 2026-12-11
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood Solutions); Tom Ellis (CTO, Harbor Tech), Marta Ruiz (IT Ops), Dr. Evan Koretz (Research Lead), Sara Ng (Compliance)
summary: Discovery call to capture requirements for deploying Redwood in a physically isolated Harbor Tech facility. Discussed offline update process, hardware constraints (power, limited NVMe, no outbound internet), security/compliance (SAML, KMS, audit logs), initial pilot scope for 4 nodes, and next steps around security docs and HW inventory.
topics: security controls: KMS/HSM, SAML, audit logs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time today. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Tom (Harbor CTO): Tom here, Marta, Evan and Sara on my side.
[00:18] Alex: Great, so high level we want to understand the facility constraints, update flow and what success looks like for a private, physically isolated deployment. Priya, you want to say hi?
[00:27] Priya (Redwood SE): Hi all, Priya from Redwood, I'll be the technical lead on the design and pilot.
[00:33] Marta (IT Ops): Thanks. To be blunt, we can't have outgoing internet from the cluster — it's a locked lab.
[00:38] Priya: Understood. We have a number of customers in fully isolated sites; usually that means air-gapped updates via signed bundles and an operator-run USB or on-site transfer.
[00:48] Sara (Compliance): We need to make sure any transfer mechanism is auditable. We can't accept a manual blob with no integrity proofs.
[00:56] Alex: Right. We provide a signed artifact model bundle and a checksum + signature you can verify with our public cert. We'll also include a manifest for versions.
[01:08] Tom: How does key management work? We have an HSM on prem and strict KMS policies, we can't export private keys.
[01:16] Priya: Redwood Private can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. The control plane in your VPC will be configured to use your key for signing local artifacts; nothing leaves the facility unencrypted. That said, the initial onboarding does require an operator to bring signed images in — the signing operation can be performed by your HSM.
[01:33] Evan (Research): Are there any online callbacks to Redwood for telemetry?
[01:38] Jordan (Redwood Solutions): For fully offline deployments telemetry can be buffered locally and pushed out only through a scheduled outbound gateway you control, or completely disabled. We also support a local-only console that never phones home.
[01:51] Marta: Good. Another constraint: our racks are older — GPUs are 40GB A100s and we only have 4 PCIe lanes open per node, and just 4TB NVMe per host.
02:01 Priya: Ok, that informs quantization and KV-cache planning. For large context models, KV caching eats NVMe; with 4TB we can host X tokens depending on model and quantization. We'll need your typical sequence lengths.
[02:17] Tom: Typical context is 4k tokens, sometimes 16k for specialized docs. We want reasonable latency, sub-200ms for short prompts, but willing to tradeoff some latency for cost.
[02:29] Alex: That lines up with Dedicated configs where we pick model variants and quantization profiles. We'll test on your HW during the pilot to tune batch sizes.
[02:38] Sara: Regarding audits: we need immutable audit logs and role separation — RBAC mapping into our SSO.
[02:45] Priya: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for user sync. Audit logs can be written to a local syslog collector and also appended to an immutable storage volume. We can also integrate with your SIEM.
[02:58] Marta: Can we get an offline installer and step-by-step ops runbook? Our on-call team will own patching, not Redwood.
[03:06] Priya: Absolutely. We provide an operator runbook, a set of orchestration containers, and an offline CLI for apply/update. The runbook describes the signed bundle verification, canary procedure and rollback.
[03:18] Tom: Rollback in a locked environment is scary — what's the fallback if a model induces bad outputs in production?
[03:25] Alex: We recommend a staged rollout even on-prem: canary one node, monitor quality with your evaluation prompts locally, then roll to remaining nodes. If things go wrong, the operator can revert to previous signed bundle.
[03:36] Evan: What's the model catalog like — do we have to take large LLMs? We're more interested in tuned smaller models for inference efficiency.
[03:44] Priya: You can pick from our curated catalog or bring your own model as a TARball. For on-prem we support quantized weights (4/8-bit) and runtime kernels optimized for those formats.
[03:55] Tom: Licenses — if we bring an open model, do we still pay per-token?
[03:59] Alex: For Private deployments pricing is typically node/seat + support and optional model licensing — for BYO open models we don't charge per-token, we charge for the deployment and support. We'll share a pricing sheet.
[04:12] Marta: What's the upgrade window? We have maintenance windows every Wednesday 01:00–05:00 local.
[04:17] Priya: We can schedule upgrades for that window. Offline bundles can be staged for your maintenance window and applied via the CLI.
[04:26] Sara: One more compliance thing: do you produce attestations for deployed versions? We need to show what exact binaries and model checksums were on a given date.
[04:35] Jordan: We can produce a deployment attestation artifact — signed manifest with checksums and the operator identity that applied it. That will be included in the security pack.
[04:46] Tom: Network design: we don't want any DNS resolution to external hosts. How do licensing/periodic heartbeats work?
[04:53] Alex: For fully air-gapped we offer token-based licenses that are bound to a hardware fingerprint and can be refreshed via signed bundles you import. No outbound heartbeat required.
[05:04] Marta: Power and thermal — some of our racks are constrained. Do you have guidance on GPU density and thermal profiles?
[05:11] Priya: We'll share a hardware sizing doc but preliminarily fewer GPUs per rack or additional cooling might be necessary for sustained throughput. We'll need the exact node SKUs.
[05:23] Tom: For the pilot we want 4 nodes sitting in one rack. The idea is to validate latency and inference throughput with our 4k/16k workloads.
[05:31] Alex: Good ping. Pilot success criteria?
[05:34] Evan: Throughput of 60 tokens/sec sustained per node for standard prompts and 200ms median latency for <512 token prompts. Also stable KV cache behavior over 24h.
[05:48] Priya: We'll capture load tests and a benchmark script. We'll also run a model degradation test with your eval prompts.
[05:56] Tom: How long does the pilot typically take?
[05:59] Alex: Usually 4 weeks: week 0 on-site prep and hardware validation, week 1 baseline tests, week 2 model tuning, week 3 handover + ops runbook and final report.
[06:12] Marta: Realistically we can be ready by end of Jan if procurement clears. We need your HW inventory template to lock that down.
[06:19] Jordan: We'll send the template after this call.
[06:22] Sara: Security review — do you have an on-site audit playbook? We sometimes get auditors who need to verify chain of custody for images.
[06:32] Priya: Yes, the pack includes chain-of-custody guidance for signed artifacts and recommended procedures for physical transfers.
[06:39] Tom: Any known limitations with older kernel versions? We're stuck on RHEL 7.9 in parts of the facility.
[06:46] Priya: Some runtime optimizations expect newer kernels for MIG and certain NVMe drivers. We can run a compatibility check; in some cases the runtime falls back to CPU paths, but that will affect latency. We'll capture specifics in the checklist.
[06:58] Evan: Regarding data residency — inference traces must never leave the facility. Will Redwood enforce that?
[07:03] Alex: For private deployments we can restrict any telemetry to local storage. If you ever want to export for debugging you opt-in and produce a signed export.
[07:12] Marta: We also want to ensure logs are retained for 2 years and are tamper-evident.
[07:17] Jordan: We'll show options: write-once volumes, hash chains for logs, or integration with your existing WORM storage.
[07:28] Tom: From a procurement perspective, what's the lead time on hardware and support?
[07:33] Alex: Once the PO lands, typical shipping and staging for a 4-node private kit is 6–8 weeks; if you already have compatible nodes, onboarding can be much faster. Support SLAs can be negotiated; standard enterprise is 24x7 with 4hr response for critical.
[07:49] Evan: Benchmarks — we've had poor experience with vendor X who claimed 2x throughput but it was synthetic. How do you run honest throughput tests?
[07:57] Priya: We use your real prompt set and synthetic stress tests. We'll run both cold-start and warmed KV-cache scenarios and provide raw logs. If you want, we can side-by-side against a reproducible baseline.
[08:09] Marta: Do you allow us to bring our own orchestration (k8s)?
[08:14] Priya: We support both k8s and our bundled runtime. For k8s we provide a Helm chart and operator that respects offline constraints; for very locked setups we can run the runtime as containers managed by your local orchestrator.
[08:27] Tom: Any special handling for GPU driver updates?
[08:31] Priya: Driver updates are operator-managed. Redwood will certify driver/model/runtime combos and provide the certified bundles; you apply them during maintenance windows.
[08:40] Alex: Time for open questions or weird edge cases?
[08:44] Sara: We need documentation for legal: transfer agreements for signed bundles and a clause about liability for model hallucinations.
[08:53] Alex: We can provide standard T&Cs and a model use addendum. We'll flag that to legal.
[08:59] Tom: Competitors — who else should we be benchmarking?
[09:03] Evan: We've looked at ModelForge and Nebula, mainly for licensing terms.
[09:08] Priya: We'll include a comparison doc that focuses on offline deployment feature parity.
[09:13] Marta: Anything else on sizing? Storage I/O is a big concern for us — 4TB NVMe shared across models could be tight.
[09:22] Priya: We'll include a mapping: model variant -> estimated NVMe and RAM footprint. We also recommend a small local cache node if you need large KV persistence.
[09:33] Alex: Okay, to recap: we'll send security pack, HW inventory template, pilot scope and pricing. Marta will send hardware details. Priya will draft pilot test plan.
[09:44] Tom: Sounds good. One last quick thought: we may need a completely offline operator UI — can you demo that in the pilot?
[09:52] Priya: Yes, we can include the local UI and CLI in the pilot.
[09:56] Alex: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a proposed date for the on-site readiness call.
[10:05] Tom: Thanks all.
[10:07] (call ends)
notes: Artifacts mentioned: Redwood security pack (link provided after call), hardware inventory template, pilot benchmark scripts
